cosy-lesson.title: AI and Art: Can machines be truly creative?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: to introduce the topic and clarify key target vocabulary for the session.

cosy-slide.cosy-instruction: Review the key vocabulary for this session below:

cosy-blockquote.p: Originality – the ability to think independently and creatively.

p.em: Example: The designer's work is known for its originality.

cosy-blockquote.p: Aesthetic – concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty.

p.em: Example: The painting has a very modern aesthetic.

cosy-blockquote.p: Canvas – a strong, coarse unbleached cloth used as a surface for painting.

p.em: Example: The artist prepared the canvas before starting to paint.

cosy-blockquote.p: Masterpiece – a work of outstanding artistry, skill, or workmanship.

p.em: Example: Many consider the Mona Lisa to be Da Vinci's masterpiece.

cosy-blockquote.p: Inspiration – the process of being mentally stimulated to do or feel something creative.

p.em: Example: Travel is a great source of inspiration for many artists.

cosy-blockquote.p: Generative – having the power or function of generating, producing, or reproducing.

p.em: Example: Generative AI can create completely new images from text.

cosy-blockquote.p: Subjective – based on or influenced by personal feelings, tastes, or opinions.

p.em: Example: Art is highly subjective; what one person loves, another may hate.

cosy-blockquote.p: Craftsmanship – skill in a particular craft.

p.em: Example: You can see the incredible craftsmanship in this handmade furniture.

cosy-blockquote.p: Copyright – the exclusive legal right to reproduce, publish, sell, or distribute a work.

p.em: Example: There are many legal battles over AI and copyright.

cosy-blockquote.p: Provocative – causing annoyance, anger, or another strong reaction, especially deliberately.

p.em: Example: The artist is known for his provocative and controversial works.

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: pair/group discussion on core session themes.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs or small breakout groups, discuss the following questions:

ol.li:
A: AI can generate unexpected combinations, sparking a new kind of creative originality. B: True originality requires human consciousness, emotion, and life experience.
★ How do you define originality when evaluating a piece of art?

A: Machine algorithms can analyze millions of images to produce a perfect aesthetic balance. B: A refined aesthetic sensibility is a uniquely human quality developed over centuries of culture.
★ What kind of visual aesthetic appeals to you the most in modern design?

A: Digital screens serve as a limitless, modern canvas for complex algorithmic art. B: The physical texture of paint on a real canvas connects the viewer directly to the artist's touch.
★ Do you prefer digital illustrations or traditional paintings on a physical canvas?

A: AI can help amateur creators produce a visual masterpiece with minimal technical training. B: A true masterpiece requires years of dedicated struggle, discipline, and human genius.
★ Have you ever stood in front of a famous masterpiece and felt deep emotion?

A: Artists can use generative tools as a source of instant inspiration to overcome creative blocks. B: Genuine inspiration comes from real-world interactions, suffering, and existential reflection (e.g. contemplating mortality, love, or individual purpose).
★ Where do you find your greatest creative inspiration?

A: Modern generative models democratize the creative process, allowing everyone to build art. B: Relying on generative systems turns art into a repetitive commodity.
★ Have you ever experimented with any generative AI tools to create images or text?

A: Art is highly subjective, so machine-made art is just as valid as human-made art. B: The subjective depth of human communication through art cannot be replicated by numbers.
★ Do you agree that the value of any artwork is entirely subjective?

A: AI can replicate complex historical styles with flawless digital craftsmanship. B: Real human craftsmanship lies in the beautiful imperfections of physical labor.
★ Do you value technical craftsmanship or the underlying concept more in art?

A: Open-source AI models promote collaborative creativity by moving past rigid copyright laws. B: Protecting intellectual property via strict copyright is essential for artists to survive financially.
★ Do you think AI companies should pay royalties for using copyright material in their training?

A: Algorithmic art can be highly provocative, forcing us to redefine what creativity means. B: True art should be provocative through human intention, not random mathematical variation.
★ What is the most provocative or challenging artwork you have ever seen?

cosy-teacher-notes.p: Stage aim: deeper debate and statement evaluation in pairs/groups.

cosy-slide.cosy-group-instruction: In pairs, debate and state whether you agree or disagree with these statements:

ol.li:
A: AI art is based on pattern replication, which destroys the very concept of originality. B: Human artists often copy their mentors, which is no different from AI originality limits.
★ If an AI mimics a human style perfectly, does it possess any genuine originality?

A: Algorithms tend to produce a standardized, lifeless aesthetic that makes all art look similar. B: Human taste is also shaped by media trends, creating a highly commercialized aesthetic.
★ Does the standard aesthetic of AI-generated images feel cold or artificial to you?

A: The death of the physical canvas isolates viewers from the tactile nature of real artwork. B: Traditional canvas materials are expensive and limit art accessibility to wealthy classes.
★ Do you think the physical canvas will eventually disappear in favor of digital screens?

A: Flooding the market with cheap digital files devalues the status of a classic masterpiece. B: The elitist art market artificially inflates the price of any human-made masterpiece.
★ Does a digital image have the potential to be considered a historical masterpiece?

A: Laziness increases when creators rely on AI prompts rather than internal inspiration. B: Modern life is so exhausting that artists need technological tools to spark their inspiration.
★ Do you worry that over-reliance on technology will dry up human inspiration?

A: Uncontrolled generative tools threaten to replace professional graphic designers and illustrators. B: Resisting generative technology is futile and harms the development of modern digital design.
★ Should schools ban the use of generative models in art and design classes?

A: Removing the subjective soul of the artist leaves AI art empty and meaningless. B: Human interpretation is so subjective that the creator's true identity is irrelevant to the viewer.
★ Can you appreciate an artwork even if you know nothing about its subjective origin?

A: A society that relies on algorithms will lose the physical skill of manual craftsmanship. B: Traditional craftsmanship can be slow, inefficient, and inaccessible for urgent commercial projects.
★ Do you worry that manual craftsmanship is becoming a lost art in our digital age?

A: AI models are built on massive, unauthorized copyright infringement. B: Outdated copyright laws block scientific and creative progress in the digital era.
★ How should society protect artists' copyright in the age of neural networks?

A: Randomly generated images are often offensive or empty rather than genuinely provocative. B: Keeping art safe and non-provocative leads to cultural stagnation.
★ Do you think art has a responsibility to be provocative, or should it focus on beauty?

ul.li: Incorrect: The machine can't replace a real artist → Correct: Machines can't replace real artists ((Generalization with plurals))
Incorrect: I've been interested to art since 5 years → Correct: I've been interested in art for 5 years ((Preposition + Duration))
Incorrect: It doesn't makes sense → Correct: It doesn't make sense ((Dependent on))

Incorrect: I am very sensible to beautiful aesthetic designs → Correct: I am very sensitive to beautiful aesthetic designs ((False friend: 'sensible' means having good judgment, while 'sensitive' means highly responsive or emotionally receptive to something))
Incorrect: I didn't expect the AI could paint so good → Correct: I didn't expect the AI could paint so well ((Use the adverb 'well' to modify the verb 'paint', as 'good' is an adjective))
